title: Instant Pot Dominican-Style Sancocho with Chicken, Pork & Root Vegetables
dek: A two-stage pressure-cooker stew turns pork, chicken, plantain, yuca, squash and corn into a deeply savory family meal without sacrificing the vegetables' shape.
image_alt: Dominican-style sancocho with pieces of chicken and pork and a corn round in a thick green-brown root-vegetable broth, served with white rice and lime
ingredients: 1 1/4 lb boneless pork shoulder, cut into 1 1/2-inch pieces
1 1/4 lb boneless skinless chicken thighs, cut into 2-inch pieces
2 tbsp chopped cilantro stems, plus leaves for serving
1 tbsp fresh lime juice, plus lime wedges for serving
1 green plantain, peeled and cut into 1-inch pieces
12 oz frozen peeled yuca, cut into 1 1/2-inch pieces
12 oz calabaza or butternut squash, peeled and cut into 1 1/2-inch pieces
2 ears corn, each cut crosswise into 4 rounds
2 cups cooked white rice, for serving
Hot sauce or sliced fresh chile, optional for serving

instructions.name: Season the meats
instructions.text: Pat pork and chicken dry. Toss the pork with 3/4 teaspoon salt and half the oregano; season the chicken with 1/2 teaspoon salt and the remaining oregano. Keep the meats on separate plates and wash hands and surfaces after handling.

instructions.name: Brown the pork
instructions.text: Select Sauté on Normal on a 6-quart electric pressure cooker. Heat 1 tablespoon oil and brown the pork in two batches for about 3 minutes per batch. Transfer to a plate; the pork need not be cooked through.

instructions.name: Build and deglaze the base
instructions.text: Add the remaining oil, onion and bell pepper and cook 4 minutes. Stir in garlic, cilantro stems and tomato paste for 45 seconds, then cancel Sauté. Pour in 3 cups broth and scrape until the base is completely smooth. Stir in lime juice and return the pork with its juices.

instructions.name: Pressure-cook the pork
instructions.text: Lock the lid and cook on High Pressure for 18 minutes; allow about 15 minutes to reach pressure. Let pressure release naturally for 10 minutes, then vent the remainder in short controlled pulses. Pause if liquid sputters and open only after the float valve drops.

instructions.name: Layer the chicken and vegetables
instructions.text: Stir the broth, then add plantain and yuca. Arrange chicken, squash and corn on top and pour the remaining 1 cup broth down the side. Do not pack the pot above its maximum-fill line. Do not stir the squash into the base.

instructions.name: Finish under pressure
instructions.text: Lock the lid and cook on High Pressure for 6 minutes; allow 10 to 12 minutes to repressurize. Let pressure release naturally for 10 minutes, then use a controlled release for any remainder. Open only when the float valve drops.

instructions.name: Verify and thicken
instructions.text: Check several chicken pieces for 165°F and pork pieces for at least 145°F; the pork should also yield easily to a fork. If needed, simmer on Sauté Low until safe and tender. Mash several pieces of squash and plantain into the broth, then season with the remaining 3/4 teaspoon salt as needed.

instructions.name: Serve the family bowls
instructions.text: Ladle meat, vegetables, corn and thick broth into wide bowls. Add rice alongside, finish with cilantro and lime, and offer hot sauce or chile at the table so the shared pot stays mild.

why_it_works: Pork gets a head start under pressure, while chicken and the softer vegetables enter for a shorter second cycle.
Four cups of thin broth and a thoroughly scraped base provide reliable steam while tomato paste stays diluted instead of scorching.
Mashing only a few cooked vegetables gives sancocho its full body without flour or an over-reduced pressure stage.
swaps: Use all chicken thighs for a pork-free stew; skip the first pressure cycle and cook the full layered pot for 9 minutes with a 10-minute natural release.
Taro or malanga can replace an equal weight of yuca; keep chunks large and inspect for tenderness after pressure.
Serve with avocado instead of rice for a lighter plate, without changing the liquid inside the cooker.
storage: Cool stew and rice in separate shallow containers within 2 hours. Refrigerate for up to 4 days or freeze the stew without rice for up to 3 months. Thaw in the refrigerator and reheat to 165°F, adding broth because the root vegetables continue to thicken it.
notes: Total time includes two pressurizing periods, both programmed cycles, two 10-minute natural releases, controlled venting and finishing time.
Written for a 6-quart electric pressure cooker. Follow your model manual for minimum liquid, maximum fill and venting, and never force the lid.
Keep the pot below the maximum-fill line. This recipe contains neither grains nor dried beans, but it still should not be doubled in a 6-quart cooker.
Frozen peeled yuca is convenient and avoids the fibrous peel; remove any tough central core that remains after cooking.
The base is intentionally mild. Put hot sauce and sliced chile on the table, not in the family pot.

faqs.q: Why are there two pressure cycles?
faqs.a: Pork shoulder needs longer to become tender than chicken, squash and corn. Staging them prevents dry chicken and disintegrated vegetables.
Yes. Use 1 1/2 pounds bone-in thighs and keep the six-minute second cycle. Check beside—but not touching—the bone for 165°F.
It should be spoonable but fuller-bodied than a clear soup. Mash a little more plantain or squash for extra body, or add hot broth if it becomes too thick.

title: Instant Pot Italian-Style Creamy Polenta with Mushrooms & Parmesan
dek: Pot-in-pot pressure cooking keeps coarse cornmeal off the heating element while a skillet of deeply browned mushrooms makes this meatless dinner feel complete.
image_alt: Creamy yellow polenta topped with glossy browned mushroom pieces and herbs on a white plate
ingredients: 1 1/2 cups water, for the pressure-cooker base
1 1/2 lb mixed mushrooms, sliced 1/3 inch thick
1 cup finely grated Parmesan, plus more for serving
Crushed red pepper, optional for serving

instructions.name: Choose the inner bowl
instructions.text: Set a trivet in a 6-quart electric pressure cooker and test that a 2 1/2- to 3-quart heatproof stainless-steel bowl sits securely on it with clearance for the lid. Remove the bowl and trivet.

instructions.name: Whisk the polenta
instructions.text: In the inner bowl, whisk polenta, 5 cups water, vegetable broth, 1 teaspoon salt and 1 tablespoon olive oil until no dry pockets remain. The bowl must be less than half full because cornmeal expands.

instructions.name: Load for pot-in-pot cooking
instructions.text: Pour 1 1/2 cups water into the cooker liner and set in the trivet. Lower the uncovered polenta bowl onto the trivet. The polenta never touches the heated liner, which reduces burn-warning risk.

instructions.name: Pressure-cook and release
instructions.text: Lock the lid and cook on High Pressure for 10 minutes; allow about 10 minutes to reach pressure. Let pressure release naturally for 15 minutes, then vent any remainder in short controlled pulses. Pause if steam sputters and open only after the float valve drops.

instructions.name: Brown the mushrooms
instructions.text: While the cooker runs, heat the remaining oil in a 12-inch skillet over medium-high. Brown mushrooms in two batches for 5 to 7 minutes each. Return all mushrooms, add shallots, garlic, thyme and the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt, and cook 3 minutes. Stir in balsamic vinegar and remove from heat.

instructions.name: Finish the polenta
instructions.text: Using heat-safe mitts, lift out the hot bowl. Whisk thoroughly until smooth, then whisk in butter and Parmesan. It should flow slowly from the whisk; add hot water 2 tablespoons at a time if thicker than desired.

instructions.name: Plate the dinner
instructions.text: Spoon polenta onto warm plates and top with the glossy mushrooms as shown in the photograph. Finish with parsley and Parmesan, and offer crushed red pepper separately so the base stays family-friendly.

why_it_works: The pot-in-pot method isolates expanding cornmeal from the cooker's heating element and preserves a generous thin-liquid reservoir below.
A 15-minute natural release lets coarse polenta finish hydrating before vigorous whisking smooths it.
Cooking mushrooms in batches drives off moisture quickly, creating browned flavor instead of a watery topping.
swaps: Use pecorino Romano for a sharper finish, but reduce the added salt because it is saltier than Parmesan.
For vegan polenta, use plant butter and nutritional yeast or a vegan hard cheese; verify the broth is vegan.
Cremini mushrooms alone work well if a mixed mushroom package is unavailable.
storage: Cool polenta and mushrooms in separate shallow containers within 2 hours and refrigerate for up to 4 days. Reheat polenta to steaming hot with a splash of water or broth, whisking often; warm mushrooms separately. Chilled polenta may also be sliced and pan-crisped. Freeze for up to 2 months, though texture softens.
notes: Total time includes about 10 minutes to pressurize, the 10-minute cycle, a 15-minute natural release and mushroom preparation done in parallel.
Written for a 6-quart electric pressure cooker. Confirm your manual permits pot-in-pot cooking and follow its trivet, minimum-liquid, fill-limit and release guidance.
Use an uncovered metal bowl rated for pressure cooking. Never seal a separate container inside the cooker.
Keep the polenta bowl below half full and the cooker liner below its maximum-fill line.
The pot stays mild; crushed red pepper is an optional table condiment.

faqs.a: No. Instant polenta hydrates too quickly for this pressure cycle. Use coarse-ground cornmeal labeled polenta and follow its package ratio if it differs substantially.

faqs.q: Why is the inner bowl left uncovered?
faqs.a: An uncovered bowl allows steam to heat the mixture evenly. Foil slows hydration and can trap condensation; the generous bowl size prevents splashing.

faqs.q: What if the polenta looks separated when I open the lid?
faqs.a: That is normal. Whisk it firmly for 30 to 60 seconds before adding butter and cheese; the hydrated grains will become creamy.

title: Finnish Lohikeitto with Salmon, Potatoes & Dill
dek: Salmon cooks gently in a leek-and-potato broth enriched with cream, fresh dill and allspice for a restorative Nordic soup that reaches the table in under an hour.
image_alt: Finnish salmon soup with large pink salmon pieces, diced potatoes, carrot, leek and dill in a golden creamy broth
ingredients: 2 large leeks, white and pale-green parts halved, rinsed and sliced
1 1/2 lb Yukon Gold potatoes, peeled and cut into 3/4-inch cubes
6 cups low-sodium fish stock or vegetable broth
1 1/2 lb skinless salmon fillet, pin bones removed, cut into 1 1/2-inch pieces

instructions.name: Sweat the leeks
instructions.text: Melt butter in a heavy 5-quart pot over medium-low. Add leeks and carrots with 1/2 teaspoon salt and cook 6 to 8 minutes, stirring, until softened but not browned.

instructions.name: Simmer the potatoes
instructions.text: Add potatoes, stock, allspice and bay leaves. Bring to a boil, reduce to a steady simmer and cook partially covered for 12 to 15 minutes, until a potato cube is nearly tender but still holds its shape.

instructions.name: Poach the salmon gently
instructions.text: Season salmon with 1/2 teaspoon salt. Lower the heat so the broth barely simmers, add salmon in one layer and cook 4 to 6 minutes without vigorous stirring. Check several thick pieces; each must reach 145°F.

instructions.name: Enrich without boiling
instructions.text: Stir in cream and half the dill. Warm over low heat for 2 to 3 minutes until steaming, but do not boil. Remove allspice berries and bay leaves.

instructions.name: Balance and serve
instructions.text: Stir in lemon juice, pepper and the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt, then taste. Ladle the golden creamy broth with visible salmon, potatoes, carrot and leek into bowls as photographed. Finish with remaining dill and serve with rye bread.

why_it_works: Potatoes cook before salmon enters, allowing the fish to poach briefly rather than break apart during a long simmer.
Cream is added over low heat after the salmon is safe, reducing the chance of scorching or curdling.
Whole allspice and fresh dill bring traditional Nordic fragrance while lemon keeps the rich broth lively.
swaps: Arctic char or skinless steelhead trout can replace salmon with the same 145°F target.
Use half-and-half for a lighter broth; avoid boiling because lower-fat dairy separates more readily.
Waxy red potatoes can replace Yukon Golds and retain a slightly firmer shape.
storage: Cool in shallow containers within 2 hours and refrigerate for up to 3 days. Reheat gently on the stovetop to 165°F without boiling so the salmon remains tender. Freezing is not recommended because potatoes become grainy and cream may separate.
notes: Rinse between leek layers after slicing to remove hidden grit.
Remove salmon pin bones with clean tweezers before cutting the fillet.
Keep the liquid at a bare simmer after adding salmon; hard boiling breaks the fish into dry flakes.
Fish must reach 145°F in the thickest pieces; leftovers should reach 165°F.
Fish stock varies in salt, so reserve the final seasoning until the cream is incorporated.

faqs.a: Yes. Thaw it completely in the refrigerator, pat dry and cut evenly before poaching. Do not add frozen blocks directly because the potatoes would overcook before the center reaches 145°F.
The soup probably boiled after the cream was added. Remove the pot from high heat, use full-fat cream and warm it only until steaming.

faqs.q: Can I make the soup ahead?
faqs.a: For the best texture, prepare the soup through the potato stage, chill it, then reheat and poach fresh salmon before adding cream and dill.

title: South Indian-Style Masala Dosa with Spiced Potato Filling
dek: An overnight rice-and-lentil batter cooks into lacy, golden crepes wrapped around mustard-seed potatoes, with precise fermentation and griddle cues for a rewarding weekend project.
image_alt: Large lacy South Indian-style dosa spread open on a dark plate with a mound of yellow spiced potato filling in the center
ingredients: 2 cups parboiled rice or idli rice
1 3/4 to 2 cups filtered water, plus more for soaking
3 tbsp neutral oil, plus more for the griddle
1 serrano chile, seeded and minced, optional
Coconut chutney and sambar, optional for serving

instructions.name: Soak rice and lentils
instructions.text: Rinse rice until the water is mostly clear, then cover it with 3 inches of water. In a separate bowl, rinse urad dal and fenugreek, then cover with 3 inches of water. Soak both for 5 to 6 hours.

instructions.name: Blend a smooth batter
instructions.text: Drain, reserving some soaking water. Blend urad dal and fenugreek with about 3/4 cup filtered water until very smooth and aerated. Transfer to a large nonreactive bowl. Blend rice and cooked rice with 1 cup water until smooth with a faint sandy texture. Mix both batters by hand; it should pour in a thick ribbon.

instructions.name: Ferment safely
instructions.text: Cover loosely and ferment in a warm 75–85°F spot for 8 to 12 hours, until visibly risen, bubbly and pleasantly tangy. Discard if it develops pink, orange or fuzzy growth or a rotten odor. Stir in 1 teaspoon salt and enough water to make a pourable pancake-like batter.

instructions.name: Cook and crush the potatoes
instructions.text: Cover potatoes with cool salted water, bring to a simmer and cook 18 to 22 minutes until tender. Drain, cool enough to handle, peel if desired and break into rough 1-inch pieces.

instructions.name: Temper the filling
instructions.text: Heat 3 tablespoons oil in a wide skillet over medium. Add mustard seeds and cover until popping slows. Add cumin and curry leaves for 20 seconds, then onion, ginger and optional serrano. Cook 7 to 9 minutes until soft. Stir in turmeric.

instructions.name: Finish the potato masala
instructions.text: Fold in potatoes, 1/2 cup water and the remaining 3/4 teaspoon salt. Crush about one-third of the potatoes and cook 5 minutes until cohesive but chunky. Stir in lemon and cilantro. Keep warm; offer extra chile separately for a mild family batch.

instructions.name: Season the griddle
instructions.text: Heat a cast-iron or nonstick griddle over medium until a drop of water dances and evaporates. Wipe with a very thin film of oil, then lower the heat briefly; too much oil prevents the batter from spreading.

instructions.name: Spread and crisp each dosa
instructions.text: Pour a scant 1/2 cup batter in the center and immediately spiral outward with the bottom of the ladle into a thin 10- to 12-inch circle. Drizzle 1/2 teaspoon oil around the edge. Cook 2 to 3 minutes until the underside is golden and the surface looks dry; no flip is needed.

instructions.name: Fill and serve immediately
instructions.text: Place about 1/2 cup potato masala in the center, matching the photographed open presentation, or fold the crisp dosa over it. Repeat, cooling and lightly wiping the griddle between dosas if batter stops spreading. Serve at once with optional chutney and sambar.

why_it_works: Blending rice and urad dal separately gives the rice enough texture for crispness while the dal becomes airy enough to support fermentation.
A warm but not hot fermentation develops lift and tang without commercial yeast.
A nearly dry, moderately hot griddle lets batter grip and spread thinly before oil crisps the underside.
swaps: Use short-grain rice if idli rice is unavailable, though the dosa may be slightly less crisp.
For a chile-free filling, omit serrano and serve chile chutney only to diners who want heat.
Sweet potatoes can replace up to half the Yukon Golds for a sweeter, softer filling.
storage: Refrigerate fermented batter and potato filling separately for up to 4 days. Bring batter toward room temperature and thin as needed before cooking; reheat filling to 165°F. Cooked dosas lose crispness quickly and are best fresh. Freeze batter in measured containers for up to 1 month, leaving room for expansion.
notes: Total time includes 6 hours soaking, about 12 hours fermenting and 1 hour 40 minutes active preparation and cooking.
Fermentation speed depends on room temperature; look for visible rise, bubbles and a clean tangy aroma rather than following the clock alone.
Use filtered water if heavily chlorinated tap water slows fermentation in your kitchen.
Cool the griddle briefly between dosas if the batter sets before it can be spread.
The batter is naturally gluten-free, but verify spices, chutney and serving accompaniments if cooking for someone with celiac disease.

faqs.q: Why did my batter not rise?
faqs.a: The room may be cool or the dal may not have blended aerated enough. Move the bowl to a warmer 75–85°F place and give it several more hours, but discard any batter with colored growth or an unpleasant odor.

faqs.q: Why does the batter stick to the ladle?
faqs.a: The griddle is probably too hot or oily. Cool it with a brief wipe from a damp cloth, then apply only a faint film of oil before spreading again.

faqs.q: Can I shorten the process with baking soda?
faqs.a: A small pinch can lighten a sluggish batter, but it cannot replace fermentation's flavor. Plan the soak and overnight rest for the best texture.

title: German Bienenstich with Vanilla Cream & Almond Caramel
dek: A tender yeast cake bakes beneath a crackly honey-almond crown, then splits around a stable vanilla pastry-cream filling for a bakery-worthy celebration slice.
image_alt: Slice of German Bienenstich with two tender yeast-cake layers, a thick pale vanilla-cream center and a glossy sliced-almond caramel top
ingredients: 3 1/4 cups all-purpose flour (390 g), plus more for the pan
For the almond topping: 6 tbsp unsalted butter
For the filling: 2 cups whole milk
1 vanilla bean, split and scraped, or 2 tsp vanilla extract

instructions.name: Mix and knead the dough
instructions.text: Combine flour, yeast, sugar and salt in a mixer bowl. Add warm milk and eggs; mix on low until shaggy. Knead with the dough hook 4 minutes, then add softened butter a tablespoon at a time. Knead 6 to 8 minutes more until smooth, elastic and slightly tacky.

instructions.name: Let the dough rise
instructions.text: Transfer to a lightly buttered bowl, cover and rise in a warm place for 60 to 90 minutes, until doubled. Meanwhile, butter and flour a 9-inch springform pan and line the base with parchment.

instructions.name: Prepare the vanilla pastry cream
instructions.text: Bring milk, 1/4 cup sugar and vanilla bean and seeds to steaming. Whisk yolks, remaining 1/4 cup sugar and cornstarch in a bowl. Slowly whisk in half the hot milk, return everything to the saucepan and cook over medium, whisking, until thick and bubbling. Boil gently for 1 minute; it should register at least 180°F. Remove the pod and whisk in butter.

instructions.name: Chill the custard
instructions.text: Spread pastry cream in a shallow dish, press wrap directly onto the surface and cool 20 minutes. Refrigerate at least 2 hours, until thoroughly cold.

instructions.name: Shape and proof
instructions.text: Press risen dough evenly into the prepared pan. Cover and proof 30 to 45 minutes, until puffy and nearly doubled. Heat the oven to 350°F.

instructions.name: Cook the almond caramel
instructions.text: Melt butter, sugar, honey, cream and salt in a saucepan over medium. Bring to a gentle boil for 2 minutes, stirring, then fold in almonds. Cool 5 minutes and spoon evenly over the proofed dough without pressing it down.

instructions.name: Bake and cool completely
instructions.text: Bake 27 to 32 minutes, until the almond top is deep golden and the cake center reaches 190–195°F. Cool in the pan 15 minutes, release the sides and cool completely on a rack for about 90 minutes.

instructions.name: Lighten the filling
instructions.text: Whisk the cold pastry cream until smooth. Whip cold cream with confectioners' sugar to medium peaks, then fold it into the pastry cream in three additions. Keep chilled until assembly.

instructions.name: Split without cracking the crown
instructions.text: Use a serrated knife to slice the cake horizontally. Lift off the top and cut it into 12 wedges before filling; pre-cutting prevents the brittle almond caramel from crushing the cream later.

instructions.name: Fill, chill and serve
instructions.text: Set the bottom layer on a platter and spread the vanilla cream evenly to the edge. Arrange almond-topped wedges over the cream to reconstruct the crown. Chill 45 minutes, then slice between the pre-cut wedges for the photographed layers.

why_it_works: A butter-rich yeast dough stays tender while supporting the substantial custard filling and almond top.
One minute of bubbling activates the cornstarch fully, and folded whipped cream makes the cold pastry cream stable but light.
Cutting the caramelized crown before assembly preserves neat slices instead of forcing a knife through brittle almonds into soft cream.
swaps: Use vanilla extract after the custard comes off heat if a vanilla bean is unavailable.
Pastry flour can replace up to one-third of the all-purpose flour for an even softer crumb; do not use cake flour alone.
For a nut-free variation, use a thin honey-oat streusel, but label it as inspired by Bienenstich rather than traditional almond-topped cake.
storage: Keep assembled cake covered and refrigerated for up to 3 days because of the custard. Let slices stand 15 minutes before serving. Freeze the unfilled baked cake for up to 2 months; thaw before splitting and filling. Do not freeze the assembled cream cake because the filling can weep.
notes: Total time includes both dough rises, baking, full cooling, custard chilling and a 45-minute assembly chill.
Warm milk above 120°F can weaken yeast; use a thermometer and stay within 105–110°F.
Cook pastry cream to at least 180°F and a full gentle bubble, then chill promptly in a shallow dish.
The almond caramel is extremely hot when cooked. Keep hands and children clear until it cools on the baked cake.
A 9-inch springform pan creates the tall layer proportions shown in the photograph.

faqs.q: Why did the almond topping slide off?
faqs.a: The dough may have over-proofed or the topping was too hot and fluid. Cool caramel for 5 minutes, spoon it gently over puffy—not collapsing—dough and bake immediately.

faqs.q: Can I make Bienenstich a day ahead?
faqs.a: Yes. Assemble it the evening before, cover and refrigerate. The cream sets neatly and the almond top remains pleasantly chewy-crisp for the next day.

faqs.q: Why is my pastry cream lumpy?
faqs.a: Eggs heated too quickly or the starch was not whisked continuously. Press the hot custard through a fine sieve, then cover its surface before chilling.
